## 1. Intro

- Very common question at top companies; Evan has asked it many times himself
- Run like a real interview, with interviewer tips and per-level expectations
- The whiteboard is linked in the description
- At the time, the next video in progress was the web crawler (most voted)

## 2. Roadmap: infrastructure-style question

- Product design questions (Ticketmaster, Uber, Dropbox): requirements, core entities, API, HLD, deep dives
- This is an **infrastructure design** question: not user-facing
  - Replace core entities + API with **system interface + data flow**
- Flow
  1. Requirements: functional, and non-functional (the critical part: system qualities)
  2. System interface: what data comes in, what goes out (sets the system boundary)
  3. Data flow: the sequence of steps that turns input into output
  4. High-level design: boxes and arrows; goal is the functional requirements
  5. Deep dives: satisfy the non-functional requirements

## 3. What an ad click aggregator is

- Collects and aggregates ad-click data
- Users click ads on websites, get redirected to the ad target, and we log the click
- Advertisers see metrics: how effective the ad is, how many clicks, over which periods
- Assume ads shown on our own site or app, like Facebook (write-up)

## 4. Functional requirements

- Features of the system; "users" may be external, internal, machines, or APIs
- 1. **User clicks an ad and is redirected to the advertiser's site**
  - Click a Nike ad, land on nike.com; some nuance in how
- 2. **Advertisers query click metrics over time**
  - "My Nike campaign: clicks over the last week, hourly"; zoom into a day at minute level
  - **Minimum granularity: 1 minute**
- Out of scope (only if it comes up naturally; don't force it)
  - Ad targeting and serving (which ad shows on the page)
  - Cross-device tracking
  - Integration with offline channels
  - Only ads on our own site, not an ad network on other sites

## 5. Non-functional requirements

- Ask for scale first, especially for infra questions
  - **10M active ads** at any time
  - **10K clicks/s at peak**
- Write-up math: peak ≈ 10× average, so ~1K clicks/s average → ~100M clicks/day (write-up)
- Don't just list "-ilities"; that's "wholly uninteresting"
  - Pick the ones unique to this system, put them in context, quantify them
- Requirements
  - **Scalable** to a peak of 10K clicks/s
  - **Low-latency analytics queries**: < 1 s for advertisers
  - **Fault tolerant, high data integrity**: don't lose clicks
    - Click data can drive how much advertisers pay
  - **As real time as possible**: query data soon after the click, within the 1-minute granularity
  - **Idempotent clicks**
    - Users or bots clicking repeatedly to fake popularity
    - One user, one ad instance or placement: counts once
- Out of scope
  - Spam detection beyond idempotency (real systems use ML models)
  - Demographic profiling, conversion tracking, extra filter dimensions

## 6. System interface and data flow

- System interface: inputs and outputs, the system's boundary
  - Inputs: click data from users; queries from advertisers
  - Outputs: a redirect for users; aggregated click metrics for advertisers
  - Straightforward here, maybe skippable, but it helps build the design linearly
- Data flow
  1. Click data comes into the system
  2. User is redirected
  3. Click data is validated (idempotency)
  4. Click data is logged
  5. Click data is aggregated (into a read-optimized form)
  6. Aggregated data is queried by advertisers
- Check: the flow meets every functional requirement (steps 1, 2, 6)
- Each section feeds the next: requirements, then data flow, then HLD
- Write-up's flow is 4 steps: click, track/store, redirect, query (write-up)

## 7. High-level design

- Goal: satisfy the two functional requirements, following the data flow
- Timing: mid-level (E4/L4) reaches the HLD later; senior/staff move faster to leave time for deep dives

### 7.1 Click and redirect

- Components
  - Browser
  - **Ad Placement Service** (out of scope, kept as a black box) reads the **Ads DB**
    - Ad: adId, redirectUrl, metadata (image, text)
  - **Click Processor Service**
- Option 1: send the redirect URL with the ad (write-up: "Good")
  - Click: browser navigates to the URL; in parallel POSTs the click event
  - Problem: ad blockers or savvy users pull the URL from the DOM and skip the POST
  - Clicks go uncounted; "someone would probably build a browser extension" (write-up)
- Option 2 (chosen): send only the adId (write-up: "Great")
  1. Click sends the adId to the click processor
  2. Processor looks up the redirect URL in the Ads DB (`getRedirectUrl(adId)`)
  3. Processor logs the click
  4. Returns **302** to the redirect URL
  - Users can't bypass logging
  - Bonus: we can append tracking query parameters (out of scope)
  - Cost: added complexity; the redirect path must stay fast (write-up)

### 7.2 Query metrics: the naive version

- Evan builds up from the "crappy" mid-level answer; senior/staff should start further along
- **Click DB** stores click events: eventId, adId, userId (if logged in), timestamp
  - Real systems store much more (browser, demographics); interviews keep it simple
- **Query service** runs a query straight on the click DB
- Write-heavy store: Cassandra is the usual interview pick; many DBs work
  - Cassandra is LSM-like: writes go to an in-memory **memtable**, flushed to disk as **SSTables**
  - Write-up adds: first an append-only commit log on disk for durability (write-up)
  - SSTables are fast for single-row reads, not for range queries or aggregations
  - Knowing more internals is rarely asked
- The query

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_clicks,
       COUNT(DISTINCT UserId) AS unique_users
FROM ClickEvents
WHERE AdId = 123
  AND Timestamp BETWEEN 1640000000 AND 1640000001
```

- Slow on Cassandra, and slow on Postgres or DynamoDB too, as time windows grow
  - 10K rows/s to scan, aggregate, count
- Fails < 1 s; "would not pass" as an HLD at any level, including mid-level
  - Even when deferring to deep dives, an HLD shouldn't be this bad

### 7.3 Query metrics: batch pre-aggregation

- Key idea: pre-aggregate into a read-optimized store
- **Spark** (MapReduce) reads all click-DB shards and aggregates per minute
- **Cron scheduler** starts Spark every ~5 minutes
- Writes to an **OLAP DB**: adId, minute, totalClicks
- Query service reads the OLAP DB: fast
- OLAP may be overkill for one metric; DynamoDB or Postgres would work
  - With many query dimensions, OLAP becomes necessary
- Write-up numbers: 10K/s × 5 min = 3M events per batch × ≤100 B ≈ 300 MB (write-up)
  - Small enough for one machine; Spark gives a scalable, well-understood frame (write-up)
- Write-up: OLAP options Redshift, Snowflake, BigQuery; columnar storage makes aggregations fast (write-up)
- Write-up: why not a time-series DB (InfluxDB, TimescaleDB)? (write-up)
  - Millions of adIds and future multi-dimension slicing suit OLAP better
  - For one metric over time ranges, a TSDB is reasonable to propose
- Why two databases, not one?
  - 10K TPS isn't that much; tuned Postgres or DynamoDB can take it, with indexes for range queries
  - Still separate them
    1. **Less contention**: write-heavy and read-heavy loads don't compete for threads
    2. **Fault isolation**: a write-side outage doesn't stop reads; a read-side outage doesn't stop logging, and we can backfill
- Level read: passing for mid-level (close to fully passing); a starting point for senior/staff
- Still missing: real time, idempotency, fault tolerance

## 8. Deep dive: real time (stream processing)

- Problem: with Spark every 5 minutes, advertisers wait ~5 minutes to see results
- Run Spark more often (2.5 min, 1 min)? Startup and compute overhead set a floor
- Write-up adds: spikes make the next batch bigger, which can run past the interval and cascade (write-up)
- Write-up: a queue before the event store absorbs spikes but doesn't fix latency (write-up)
- **Replace with streaming**
  - Click processor writes to a stream: **Kinesis** (Kafka works too)
  - **Flink** reads in real time and aggregates in memory (Spark Streaming also works)
  - Per adId, per minute: "minute 45, count 12", incremented as events arrive
  - When the minute closes, write the result to the OLAP DB
  - Click DB removed (revisited later)
- **Aggregation window**: the period data is grouped over (1 minute)
- **Flush interval**: how often partial results are written (10 s)
  - The current minute shows as partial (dotted line in the UI) until complete
- Senior/staff candidates often start here; if a candidate starts with Spark, Evan pushes on the interval
- Write-up: why Flink, not plain Kafka consumers with in-memory counts? (write-up)
  - Fine for mid-level; Flink adds event-time windows, watermarks, exactly-once, state recovery
  - Event time (when the click happened) puts out-of-order events in the right minute
- Write-up: latency is similar if Spark ran every minute; the real lever is Flink can use tiny windows, Spark can't (write-up)
- Pattern: scaling writes (write-up)

## 9. Deep dive: scale to 10K clicks/s and hot shards

- Click processor and ad placement: scale horizontally on CPU/memory thresholds (e.g., 80% CPU)
  - Saying it verbally is enough; no need to draw many boxes
- Add an **API gateway** (AWS managed): routing, middleware, some load balancing
  - Each service also has its own load balancer
- **Kinesis**: limit **1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s per shard**, whichever first
  - Shard by **adId**
- **Flink**: scales horizontally; one job/task per shard, aggregating by adId
  - No cross-task contention: each task owns its adIds
- **OLAP**: shard by **advertiserId**
  - Most common query: an advertiser looks at all of their ads
  - A good place for size math (skipped in the video)
  - Write-up: managed OLAP (Snowflake, BigQuery) handles placement; ClickHouse lets you shard (write-up)
- **Hot shards**
  - Nike launches a LeBron James ad; everyone clicks; one Kinesis shard overloads
  - Higher latency; worst case, data loss
  - Fix ("celebrity problem"): partition key = `adId:0..N` for hot ads
  - The click processor must know which ads are hot (write-up: by ad spend or past click volume)
  - Video: one Flink task still owns each adId, reading across its N shards
  - Write-up: Flink strips the suffix and upserts with SUM into OLAP; concurrent writes combine (write-up)

## 10. Deep dive: fault tolerance and data integrity

- Goal: never lose click data
- Streams (Kafka, Kinesis), especially managed, are distributed and highly available; assume they're up
  - Write-up: Kafka replicates across brokers; Kinesis across AZs in a region (write-up)
- If Flink goes down: **stream retention**, e.g., **7 days**
  - Events stay after consumption; Flink resumes from its cursor/last commit and re-reads
- **Checkpointing**: the processor writes state to storage like S3 periodically
  - Helps with long windows (a day): a crash at hour 23 means re-reading 23 hours while new data arrives
  - Default interval "I think" ~15 minutes, maybe 10
  - Common senior answer "read it in a book"
  - **Here it makes no sense**: 1-minute windows mean at most a minute to replay
    - 10K/s × 60 = 600K events; not many
    - A checkpoint at 30 s barely helps and costs S3 writes
  - Rule of thumb: tiny windows (relative to event rate), skip checkpointing
  - Saying so is a staff / strong-senior signal: nuance over textbook
- **Periodic reconciliation**
  - Still possible: transient Flink errors, bad code pushes, out-of-order events
  - Rare, but any inaccuracy costs money
  - Kinesis dumps raw clicks to S3 via a connector
    - Write-up: Kafka Connect S3 Sink; Kinesis Data Firehose (write-up)
  - Cron (hourly or daily) runs Spark MapReduce over S3
  - **Reconciliation worker** compares Spark results with Flink's numbers in OLAP
    - If different, trust the batch; overwrite
    - Alert the team; monitor the mismatch rate (rising means something broke)
  - Result: real time plus high integrity

## 11. Lambda vs Kappa

- **Kappa**: everything is a stream; a single real-time layer
  - The design before reconciliation was Kappa
- **Lambda**: a real-time layer that may be inaccurate, plus a batch layer that later overwrites it
  - Accurate after the batch (e.g., 5 minutes); not before
- Video: this design is **neither**; it's a hybrid, and that's fine
  - Patterns are guidelines, not rules; adapting them shows seniority
  - Practicality over academic purity
  - Pure Lambda can pass; Evan would push on accuracy before the batch runs
- Write-up disagrees on naming: it calls this design a Lambda architecture (Flink = speed layer, Spark = batch layer) (write-up)

## 12. Deep dive: idempotent clicks

- **Idempotent**: applying an operation many times has the same effect as once
- Common answer: dedupe on userId
  - Breaks if users aren't logged in (interviewer curveball)
  - Write-up: also wrong with **retargeting**; the same ad shown again later should count again (write-up)
  - Write-up: dedupe must happen before the stream, or duplicates straddle minute windows (write-up)
- **Ad impression ID**
  - Impression = one instance of an ad being shown
  - Same Nike ad Monday and Thursday = two impressions; each may count once
  - Ad placement service generates a unique impression ID with each ad
  - Click sends adId + impressionId
- Dedupe in **Redis** (or Memcached) before writing to Kinesis
  - Seen it? Drop (maybe log). New? Accept
  - Write-up order: write to the stream first, then the cache (write-up)
    - A cache failure then means a rare duplicate, which reconciliation catches; a lost click can't be recovered
- New hole: a bot invents fresh impression IDs
  - Simple fix: store issued impression IDs and check them; costs a DB call
  - Better: **sign** the impression ID (with a timestamp) server-side
    - Placement sends adId, impressionId, signature
    - Processor verifies the signature first, then checks Redis, then writes to Kinesis
  - Write-up: HMAC over impressionId + adId, so a valid ID can't be replayed on another ad (write-up)
  - Write-up: HMAC verification costs microseconds (write-up)
- Write-up cache sizing: 100M/day × 16 B ≈ 1.6 GB, "tiny" (write-up)
  - Redis Cluster, a replica, and RDB/AOF persistence for safety (write-up)

## 13. Deep dive: low-latency queries (write-up)

- Mostly solved by pre-aggregation into OLAP (write-up)
- Long ranges (days, weeks, years) can still be slow (write-up)
  - Nightly job builds daily/weekly roll-up tables; drill down when needed (write-up)
  - A form of caching: storage traded for query speed (write-up)

## 14. What is expected at each level

- The final design is passable for **staff**
- **Senior**
  - Reconciliation could be left out
  - Might not reach idempotency
  - Needs depth somewhere: Kinesis scaling or retention policies
  - Should reach at least the Kappa design; a well-justified Lambda could pass
  - Write-up: E5 contrasts batch vs real time; picks a couple of deep dives (write-up)
- **Mid-level**
  - Even reaching this design, expect probing questions across areas
  - Answer those well and it's probably passing
  - Write-up E4 bar: knows pre-aggregation is needed; proposes at least batch (write-up)
- Breadth vs depth
  - Mid-level: 80% breadth / 20% depth
  - Senior: ~60–70 / 30–40
  - Staff: breeze through breadth, go deep
    - Often they know one area intimately from past work and teach the interviewer
    - "A telltale sign": Evan leaves having learned something
- Write-up staff bar: weighs batch vs streaming in detail; proposes fault tolerance (write-up)

## 15. Board as text (assembled from the talk)

```
Browser -> API GW -> Click Processor --302--> advertiser site
             |          |  verify sig, Redis dedupe
             |          v
             |       Kinesis (shard adId, hot: adId:0-N, 7d retention)
             |          |                    \
     Ad Placement      Flink (1 min window,   S3 raw
     (impressionId,     10 s flush)            |
      signature)        |                     Spark (daily cron)
             |          v                      |
          Ads DB      OLAP (shard advertiser) <- Reconciliation worker
                        ^
               Query Svc <- Advertiser browser
```

- Click path: verify signature, dedupe in Redis, write to Kinesis, 302 redirect
- Aggregation: Flink per adId per minute, flushes every 10 s to OLAP
- Correctness: Kinesis to S3, daily Spark re-aggregation, reconciliation worker fixes OLAP
- Earlier versions on the board: click DB (Cassandra) + 5-minute Spark batch; Kappa/Lambda notes
- Board's deep-dive list: write scale, durability/fault tolerance, dedup/data integrity, hot keys, query latency
